w: Home of Real Madrid since 1947, renamed for club president Santiago Bernabeu. A 2024 retractable-roof renovation lifted capacity to 83186, Spain's second-largest football ground behind Camp Nou. Has hosted four European Cup/Champions League finals (1957, 1969, 1980, 2010) plus the 1982 World Cup final.
s: Real Madrid's home since 1947, four Euro finals

w: Built for the 2012 Olympics as the athletics venue and ceremonies site, this Stratford ground was remodelled in 2013-2015 into a multi-purpose stadium. Home of West Ham United since 2016 and of UK Athletics, which hosts an annual Diamond League round. Capacity fell from 80000 for the Games to around 60000 for football.
s: Olympic Stadium turned West Ham's home ground

w: Ajax's home since it opened in 1996 as Amsterdam Arena, built at a cost equivalent to 140 million euros. Renamed in 2018 for Johan Cruyff, who died in 2016. Hosted the 1998 Champions League final, 2013 Europa League final and Euro 2000/2020 matches. Retractable roof; capacity 55865 for football.
s: Ajax's arena, renamed for Johan Cruyff in 2018

w: Wales's national stadium, built for the 1999 Rugby World Cup on the site of Cardiff Arms Park. Home of the Wales rugby team, retractable roof, capacity 73931 - the largest in Wales. Renamed Principality Stadium in 2016. Hosted FA Cup and League Cup finals while Wembley was rebuilt, 2001-2006.
s: Wales's national stadium, built for 1999 World Cup
_facts: home of Wales rugby union team

w: Opened 3 April 2019 on the site of the demolished White Hart Lane, Tottenham Hotspur's ground seats 62850 - the largest club stadium in London. Features the world's first dividing retractable pitch, letting a synthetic NFL surface slide beneath the grass. Construction began in 2015 after years of delay.
s: Spurs' ground with a retractable NFL pitch
_facts: capacity 62850, largest club ground in London
dividing retractable pitch for NFL games

w: Fenerbahce's home ground in Kadikoy since it opened on 17 September 1908, the first venue in the Ottoman Empire built for mass sporting events. Renovated across three spells and named for club president and Turkish PM Sukru Saracoglu. Hosted the 2009 UEFA Cup final, the last before the Europa League rebrand.

Palermo FC's home ground, known locally as La Favorita, opened in the fascist era on 24 January 1932 as Stadio Littorio - Palermo beat Atalanta 5-1 in the first match. Renamed La Favorita in 1945. A 1984 expansion added a second tier for 50000 fans; a 1990 renovation prepped it for that year's World Cup.
s: Palermo's ground, nicknamed La Favorita since 1945

w: Norwich City's home since 31 August 1935, built by the club in just 82 days after outgrowing The Nest. Near the River Wensum, it holds 27359 following the 2024 introduction of safe standing. The post-war terrace record of 43984 came in a 1963 FA Cup tie against Leicester City.
s: Norwich City's ground, built in just 82 days

w: Home of FC Red Bull Salzburg since it opened in March 2003 in Wals-Siezenheim, on Salzburg's edge, replacing the club's previous ground, Stadion Lehen. Known as the EM-Stadion Wals-Siezenheim during Euro 2008, where it staged group matches, and as Stadion Salzburg for UEFA club fixtures. Capacity 31895.
_facts: home of FC Red Bull Salzburg

w: Bologna FC's home ground in the Saragozza district, inaugurated in 1927 as Stadio Littoriale - one of the first stadiums to fold its stands into the architecture. A large arch once held a Mussolini statue, destroyed in 1943. Renamed for president Renato Dall'Ara, it hosted matches in the 1934 and 1990 World Cups.
s: Bologna's ground, opened 1927 as Stadio Littoriale

w: Headquarters of the Gaelic Athletic Association and Ireland's Gaelic games stadium since 1891, named for Archbishop Thomas Croke and known to fans as Croker. A 1991-2005 redevelopment raised capacity to 82300, Europe's 4th-largest. Hosted Ireland's rugby/football internationals 2007-2010 while Aviva Stadium was built.

Home of Besiktas, built on the site of the demolished BJK Inonu Stadium after an estimated 80 million dollar project. Also known as Besiktas Park for UEFA fixtures, it seats roughly 42684, with 144 executive suites and a 1903 Lounge. Hosted the 2019 UEFA Super Cup; set to host the 2026 Europa League final.
s: Besiktas's smart stadium, replaced Inonu Stadium

w: Birmingham City's home since 1906, built to replace the outgrown Muntz Street ground, once holding an estimated 75000 fans. The record attendance of 66844 or 67341 came in a 1939 FA Cup tie against Everton. New owners began a six-year rebuild from 1993 that made it all-seater under the Taylor Report.
_facts: known as St. Andrew's @ Knighthead Park since 2024

w: Hellas Verona's home ground, also used by the now-defunct Chievo Verona until 2021, plus women's side Bardolino Verona, rugby and athletics. Named for Veronese sports benefactor Marcantonio Bentegodi, it has 39211 total seats though only 31713 are currently approved - the eighth-largest stadium in Italy.
_facts: was also Chievo Verona's home until 2021

w: Bulgaria's second-largest stadium, named for national hero Vasil Levski and set inside Sofia's Borisova Gradina park. Seats 43230 and hosts the national team's home matches, Bulgarian Cup finals and athletics meets. Also served as Levski Sofia's Champions League venue and stages derbies between Sofia's big clubs.
s: Bulgaria's national stadium in Borisova Gradina
_facts: hosts national team and Cup finals

w: Indoor arena in Berlin's Friedrichshain district, opened in 2008 as O2 World and renamed Uber Arena in a 2024 deal with operator AEG Europe. Home of ice hockey club Eisbaren Berlin and basketball team Alba Berlin, capacity up to 17000. Hosted EuroLeague basketball Final Fours in 2009, 2016 and 2024.
s: Berlin arena, home of Eisbaren and Alba Berlin
_facts: home of Eisbaren Berlin and Alba Berlin

w: A football stadium in Riga, Latvia, built in 2000 and holding 8087 seats for spectators and VIP guests on matchdays. Ranks as the second-largest stadium in Latvia, behind Riga's own Daugava Stadium, and its design incorporates the adjoining Skonto Hall indoor arena into the same complex.

Home of HC Sparta Prague and Europe's third-largest ice hockey arena, hosting three Ice Hockey World Championships (2004, 2015, 2024), the first Laver Cup, the 2006 EuroLeague Final Four and four Fed Cup finals. Capacity reaches 20208 at its largest; also stages NHL, KHL and floorball games plus concerts.
s: Prague's arena, home of HC Sparta Prague

w: Norway's national football stadium, opened 26 September 1926 as home to FK Lyn and now owned by the Football Association of Norway. Home of Valerenga from 1999-2017, site of the Norwegian Cup final since 1948. Peak attendance of 35495 came in a 1935 match against Sweden; hosted UEFA Women's Euro finals 1987 and 1997.

Boavista's home ground in Porto's Boavista area, built atop the old Campo do Bessa stands so the club could keep playing during construction ahead of Euro 2004. Designed by Grupo3 Arquitectura, it seats 28263 and cost 45.4 million euros, over 7.7 million of which came from the Portuguese state.

Cagliari Calcio's home ground since the 2017-18 season, built in 2017 as Sardegna Arena after the closure and partial demolition of Stadio Sant'Elia. Used as a provisional ground until construction finished in 2021, when it was renamed Unipol Domus. Capacity 16416.

Real Madrid's home ground before the Santiago Bernabeu Stadium opened in 1947, built in 1924 in Madrid, Spain, and holding 22500 spectators. Inaugurated on 17 May 1924, its opening match was a 3-2 victory for Real Madrid over Newcastle United.
s: Real Madrid's ground before the Bernabeu
_facts: Real Madrid's home before Bernabeu opened 1947

w: Estonia's national athletics stadium since it opened in 1926, near Kadriorg Palace about 2km east of central Tallinn. Home of the Estonia national football team from 1926 until the 1940 Soviet occupation, and again from 1992-2000. Holds 5000 and has hosted European Athletics U23 and U20 Championships.

Valencia CF's intended replacement for the Mestalla, partially built in Benicalap, Spain, between August 2007 and February 2009 before funding ran out. After multiple redesigns, work resumed in January 2025 toward a final capacity of 70044, at an estimated cost of 250-300 million euros.
s: Valencia CF's unfinished new stadium since 2007

w: Panathinaikos's traditional home ground in the Ampelokipoi district of Athens, inaugurated in 1922 as Greece's oldest active football stadium. Also known as Leoforos Stadium, it holds 16003 and set a record attendance of 29665 for a 1967 Cup Winners' Cup tie against Bayern Munich.
_facts: inaugurated 1922, oldest active stadium in Greece
named for club president Apostolos Nikolaidis

w: Sparta Rotterdam's home ground in Rotterdam, Netherlands, popularly nicknamed Het Kasteel - Dutch for The Castle - for its imposing look. The stadium is the football club's fixed home ground for league and cup matches and holds a capacity of 11026 spectators.

St Johnstone's home ground in Perth, Scotland, since its 1989 opening, with an all-seated capacity of 10696. Has hosted the Scottish Challenge Cup final nine times and staged rugby union fixtures, including a full Scotland vs Japan international in 2004 and several Scotland A matches.
s: St Johnstone's ground in Perth since 1989
_facts: hosted Scottish Challenge Cup final 9 times
hosted Scotland vs Japan rugby international 2004

w: Indoor arena in central Birmingham, England, opened in 1991 as the National Indoor Arena - then the UK's largest - and now known as Utilita Arena Birmingham. Owned by the NEC Group near Brindleyplace. Fourth-largest UK indoor arena by capacity, with ticket sales of 530597 in 2019, the 4th-highest nationally.

Motor Lublin's home football stadium in Lublin, Poland, with a capacity of 15247 spectators. Since February 2025 it has carried the sponsored name Motor Lublin Arena, tying the naming rights to the club that plays its home matches there, though still widely known simply as Arena Lublin.

K.A.A. Gent's home ground, opened 17 July 2013 as the first newly built Belgian football stadium since 1974, replacing the Jules Ottenstadion after 93 years there. Known as Ghelamco Arena until 2024, it seats 20185. Its first competitive match, on 4 August 2013, was a 2-1 win over KV Mechelen.
s: Gent's stadium, first new Belgian ground since 1974
_facts: first newly built Belgian stadium since 1974

w: FK Dukla Prague's home ground in Prague-Dejvice, Czech Republic, seating 8150 on individual seats. Also used for athletics events, including the annual Josef Odlozil Memorial. A 2012 statue outside honours former Dukla player Josef Masopust, the 1962 European Footballer of the Year.
s: Dukla Prague's ground, honours Josef Masopust
_facts: hosts Josef Odlozil Memorial athletics meet
statue of 1962 Ballon d'Or winner Josef Masopust

w: Leyton Orient's home ground in Leyton, east London, since 1937, currently sponsored as the BetWright Stadium. Tottenham Hotspur Women have shared the ground since 2022. Record attendance of 34345 came for an FA Cup fourth-round visit by West Ham United on 25 January 1964.
_facts: Tottenham Hotspur Women share ground since 2022

w: Ruch Chorzow's home ground, built 1934-1935 for the successful Ruch Wielkie Hajduki team in the Batory district of Chorzow, Poland. Also known as the Cicha Street Stadium after its address, it is used mostly for football today, with a capacity of around 9300 people.

Cambridge United's home ground since 1932, currently known as the Cledara Abbey Stadium for sponsorship reasons, capped at 7937 spectators. Its first match was a 31 August 1932 friendly; the record crowd of 14000 attended a 1970 friendly against Chelsea marking the ground's new floodlights.
_facts: among the few English grounds historically styled 'stadium'

w: Multi-purpose indoor arena in Prague, Czech Republic, opened in 1962 with a capacity of 18500, now reduced to about 13238 for ice hockey. Hosted the Ice Hockey World Championships four times between 1972 and 1992. Home of HC Sparta Praha from 1962 to 2015, naming rights now leased to Fortuna.
_facts: hosted Ice Hockey World Championships 4 times

w: K.A.A. Gent's former home ground in Gentbrugge, Ghent, Belgium, built in 1920 and holding 12919 seats, sitting amid a residential neighbourhood on Bruiloftstraat. Replaced as the club's home ground by the new Ghelamco Arena in 2013, and known locally simply as Ottenstadion.
_facts: replaced by Ghelamco Arena (now Planet Group Arena)

w: G.D. Estoril Praia's home ground in Estoril, Portugal, hosting the Primeira Liga club's top-flight matches. Built with a nominal capacity of 8000, current seating is limited to just 5094 because the upper north stand remains closed over structural defects in its foundations.
s: Estoril Praia's ground, capped after stand closure
_facts: upper north stand closed for structural defects

w: AFC Wimbledon's home ground in Wimbledon, south-west London, since 3 November 2020, currently sponsored as the Cherry Red Records Stadium. Named the 42nd best stadium in world football in a 2024 ranking. Rugby league side London Broncos have shared the ground since 2022.
_facts: home of AFC Wimbledon since 3 Nov 2020

w: Home stadium of Atletico Madrid's reserve teams and CF Rayo Majadahonda, in Majadahonda, Community of Madrid, Spain, part of the Ciudad Deportiva Atletico de Madrid complex. Holds around 3800. Rayo Majadahonda played its first Segunda Division season at Atletico's Wanda Metropolitano, 2018-19, for lack of capacity.
s: Atletico Madrid reserves' training ground venue
_facts: home of Atletico Madrid reserve teams
part of Ciudad Deportiva Atletico de Madrid
